- Overestimate prices after recent spikes, especially when sentiment is high (e.g., >0.7) — model tends to overshoot and fail to correct.
- Underestimate prices when sentiment is low or negative (e.g., <0.4) — model misses downward momentum or fails to adjust for bearish signals.
- Lag in correction: model often delays reacting to sentiment shifts — especially when sentiment drops sharply, forecast remains elevated.
- Mean reversion bias: model overweights recent highs and underweights recent lows — forecast tends to “stick” to prior trends even when sentiment suggests reversal.
- Horizon-specific: 30-day forecasts are overly optimistic in early part of the horizon (first 5–10 days) when sentiment is volatile — model overreacts to short-term sentiment spikes.
- When sentiment is consistently high over 3–5 days, model tends to overforecast — especially if price is trending upward — but undercorrects if sentiment later turns negative.
- If sentiment drops below 0.3 after a spike, model often fails to adjust downward — underestimates downside risk.
- Forecast should be adjusted downward if sentiment is below 0.5 and price has been trending upward — model tends to ignore bearish sentiment in favor of momentum.
